title: Class & the Codification of Manners
hook: Within a minute of meeting, strangers can guess each other's social class from how they listen, and the guess quietly decides who gets the job.
why:
Class is one of the least discussed and most powerful influences on how people are read. It is carried in accent and vocabulary, in how someone holds a knife and fork, in how they sit in an interview, in whether they nod eagerly or listen with cool detachment, in what they talk about when the work stops. Most people pick up these signals within seconds, rarely notice that they are doing so, and often mistake them for signs of character or ability.

For a man moving between worlds, from a working-class home to a university, from a trade to an office, from one country's class system to another's, these codes can feel like a test nobody announced. For a man in a position to judge others, they can quietly shape who seems polished, confident and right for the job.

This chapter covers how class is written on the body, how quickly it is read from behaviour and speech, how it shapes hiring through the idea of fit, how manners work as a gate, how to read without ranking, and what it means to move between worlds. It is about accuracy as much as fairness: ease is not competence, and eagerness is not weakness.

teach.h: Class is written on the body.
teach.p:
In 1979 the French sociologist Pierre Bourdieu argued that social class is carried not only in money and education but in the body. He called it habitus: the dispositions people absorb in childhood, which become second nature. How you sit, how loudly you speak, how much space you take, what you find funny, how you eat, what you wear and how you wear it all reflect where you grew up, and they feel to their owner like simply being natural.

Much of what counts as good manners was once deliberately codified. The sociologist Norbert Elias traced how European rules about eating with forks, using napkins, not spitting or blowing one's nose at the table spread from royal courts to the wealthy and then downward over several centuries. Each new rule became a way of telling who belonged.

The important point for a reader is that these habits are learned, not innate, and that they are learned unequally. A man who grew up with formal dinners, travel and professional parents absorbed one set of codes without effort. A man who grew up elsewhere absorbed different codes, just as complex and just as meaningful in their own setting, which may be misread or looked down on in another.

Reading class signals is therefore reading upbringing, not character. The figures here sit across a table, a setting where class is often most visible: in how people hold cutlery, pour drinks, use napkins and fill silences. None of it says anything about how clever, kind or capable either of them is.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if manners and bodily habits were innate rather than learned. Bourdieu's and Elias's work, and ordinary experience of how children absorb the habits of their homes, show them to be acquired.

teach.p:
In 2009 Michael Kraus and Dacher Keltner filmed pairs of strangers getting to know each other, then showed silent sixty-second clips to observers and asked them to estimate each person's social class. The observers' estimates agreed with each other, and they predicted the participants' actual family income and their mothers' education better than chance.

What were the observers picking up? The researchers coded the clips. Participants from wealthier, more educated backgrounds showed more signs of disengagement: doodling, grooming themselves, fiddling with objects nearby. Participants from poorer backgrounds showed more signs of engagement: nodding, laughing, raising their eyebrows, looking at their partner. The observers used these cues, mostly without knowing it.

Kraus and Keltner suggested an explanation. People with more resources depend less on others for help and can afford to attend less closely. People with fewer resources rely more on social ties and have learned to attend carefully to others. Neither style is better; each is adapted to a different life.

The trouble is how the styles are read. Detached ease tends to be read as confidence and status. Eager attentiveness can be read as nervousness, deference or lower status. The figure here leans back, at ease, one arm draped over a chair. In many rooms this posture reads as confidence. It may simply be a habit learned in a home where no one needed to watch anyone closely.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if observers could not estimate social class from short silent clips. Kraus and Keltner found that their estimates predicted family income and maternal education, through cues of engagement and disengagement.
teach.pullQuote: Ease is not competence, and eagerness is not weakness.

teach.p:
Speech carries class even more strongly than posture. In 2019 Michael Kraus and his colleagues found that listeners could judge a speaker's social class better than chance after hearing just seven words, read aloud out of context. Pronunciation carried more of the information than the choice of words.

The researchers then took the finding into hiring. They recorded real candidates for a laboratory job describing themselves briefly, then asked hundreds of people with hiring experience to evaluate them from the recordings. Candidates who sounded higher class were judged more competent and a better fit for the job, and were offered higher starting salaries and bonuses, though the evaluators knew nothing about their qualifications.

Part I's chapter on the voice described how quickly people judge others from speech. This study shows one of the most consequential directions those judgments take. An accent that signals a working-class or regional background can cost a candidate money and opportunity before they have said anything about their work.

The remedy for evaluators is the one Part IV recommended for interviews: structure. Decide in advance what a good answer contains, and score the content of what people say rather than how they sound. The figure here sits upright and still, the kind of quiet presence whose voice, once he speaks, will be judged in seconds.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if listeners could not judge class from brief speech, or if those judgments had no effect on hiring. Kraus and colleagues found both: class was detected from seven words, and higher-class speakers were judged more competent and offered more money.

teach.p:
In 2012 the sociologist Lauren Rivera published a study of hiring at elite investment banks, law firms and consulting firms in the United States. She interviewed 120 people who made hiring decisions and observed a hiring committee at work.

She found that evaluators placed great weight on what they called fit: whether a candidate was someone they would enjoy spending long hours with. In practice, fit often meant similarity. Evaluators warmed to candidates who shared their leisure pursuits, such as particular sports or travel, and their style of self-presentation. Some described warming to a candidate on discovering a shared sport. Rivera found that concerns about this kind of cultural similarity often outweighed concerns about how productive a candidate would be.

The leisure pursuits and styles that signalled fit were, Rivera noted, closely tied to wealth and upbringing: expensive sports, unpaid internships, travel, a certain polish in conversation. Fit, in other words, often reproduced class.

For anyone who interviews, the lesson is to notice when liking someone is doing the work that evidence should do. Ask about the work rather than hobbies. Be wary of the warm feeling of recognition, which is often a reading of shared background. The figure here sits with arms folded, leaning back, the posture of an interviewer who has already half decided, perhaps because the candidate reminded him of himself.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if evaluators at elite firms judged candidates mainly on likely performance rather than similarity. Rivera found that cultural similarity, including shared leisure pursuits, often outweighed concerns about productivity.

teach.p:
Manners work as a gate in many settings beyond hiring: client dinners, weddings, clubs, university halls, networking events. The rules are rarely stated. Which glass is yours, when to start eating, how to hold a wine glass, what counts as small talk, how to dress for a stated or unstated code, whether to shake hands or kiss on the cheek.

People who grew up with these codes follow them without effort, which makes them invisible. People who did not have to learn them in public, often under scrutiny, while trying to concentrate on the conversation. Many describe the experience vividly: watching others to see which fork to use, feeling their accent sharpen when nervous, wondering whether a joke will land, sensing a small pause when they do something different.

That effort shows. Someone working hard to follow unfamiliar codes may seem stiff, quiet, careful or uncomfortable. A reader who does not consider class may read that discomfort as shyness, coldness or lack of ability. The effort is the same kind described earlier in this part as masking: real, tiring and invisible to those who do not need to make it.

The kindest response is not to notice. Do not correct someone's manners in front of others, do not comment on an accent, and do not treat a different style as an error. The figure here sits with hands clasped in his lap, careful and still, the posture of someone watching the table for clues.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if people from different class backgrounds found unfamiliar social codes equally easy. People who have moved between classes consistently describe the effort of learning codes others absorbed in childhood.

teach.p:
Reading class signals is unavoidable; ranking people by them is a choice. Almost everyone notices accent, clothing and manner within seconds, and noticing is not the problem. The problem begins when those signals are allowed to decide. A few practices help keep the two apart.

First, separate manner from merit. Ease, polish, a particular accent and a confident lean-back tell you about upbringing. They do not tell you about intelligence, skill, honesty or effort. Eager nodding, a regional accent and careful formality tell you the same kind of thing, in the other direction.

Second, use structure wherever decisions matter. Part IV's chapter on interviews described the evidence that structured interviews, with set questions and scored answers, predict performance better than open conversations. They also reduce the room for class signals to stand in for evidence.

Third, read your own warm and cool reactions as data about yourself. If you feel at ease with someone, ask whether it is because of what they said or because they reminded you of people you grew up with. If you feel faint discomfort, ask whether it comes from anything they did or simply from difference. The figure here takes notes, head down, the posture of an evaluator recording what was said rather than how it sounded.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if structured evaluation made no difference to the influence of class signals. Structure directs attention to the content of answers, leaving less room for accent and manner to stand in for evidence.

teach.p:
Many readers of this book will have moved between class worlds: the first in their family at university, a tradesman who became a manager, a man who married into a different background, an immigrant learning a new country's codes. Moving between worlds often means carrying two sets of habits and switching between them.

That switching is a skill, and also a cost. A later chapter in this part looks at code-switching in detail. Here, two points are worth making. First, the habits of your first world are not errors to be corrected. The attentiveness, warmth and directness many working-class men grow up with are assets in most rooms. Second, it is worth deciding consciously which codes you adopt and which you keep, rather than letting discomfort decide for you.

If you are now in a position to help others make the same move, the most useful thing you can do is explain the unwritten rules out loud and in private. Tell a new colleague how the client dinner will work, which conversations to expect, what the dress code really means. Codes that are explained lose much of their power to exclude.

The figures here work side by side on a shared task, one showing the other how something is done. Much of class mobility depends on someone being willing to show the rules rather than test for them.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if explaining unwritten rules made no difference to newcomers. People who move between class worlds consistently describe being shown the codes, rather than left to guess them, as a decisive help.

poseGallery.annotation: Ease tells you about upbringing. Score the content of answers, not how relaxed someone looks saying them.

caseStudy:
Charles, fifty-two, is a partner at a consulting firm and regularly interviews graduates. Last year he saw two candidates on the same afternoon. The first, Hugo, was relaxed and articulate, had rowed at university and spent a summer interning at a bank his uncle worked for. They talked about Italy for ten minutes. The second, Danny, had worked in a warehouse through university, spoke with a strong Liverpool accent, nodded a great deal and laughed nervously at Charles's jokes.

Charles's instinct was clear: Hugo was a natural. But the firm had recently introduced structured interviews, and when Charles scored both candidates against the set questions, Danny's answers to the case problem were noticeably stronger. Charles looked at his notes and realised that most of what he had liked about Hugo was how familiar he felt. Hugo's answers had been fluent but thin; Danny's had been hesitant at the start and then precise, with numbers, a clear structure and a sensible recommendation.

The firm hired Danny. Before his first client dinner, Charles took him aside and explained how the evening would go: who would be there, what they would talk about, how the bill would be handled, what to wear. Danny said later that it was the most useful thing anyone had told him in his first year.

Charles has started paying attention to the moment of recognition in interviews, the feeling that a candidate is someone like him, and treating it as a reason to check his scores rather than as evidence.
observe: Notice, in your next meeting with someone new, whether you feel at ease or slightly uncomfortable, and what in their manner or speech prompted it.
Notice cues of engagement and disengagement in a group: who nods and laughs, who doodles or leans back, and how each is being read.
Notice accents in your workplace, and whether some are associated with particular roles or levels of seniority.
Notice unwritten rules in a setting you know well, such as a client dinner or a club, and which of them a newcomer would have to guess.

drills.name: Ease Versus Evidence
steps: Think of someone you rated highly in a first meeting.
List what made the impression: what they said, and how they said it.
Separate the two columns: content and manner.
Ask whether your impression would survive if you had only the content.
variations: Repeat the exercise for someone you rated poorly in a first meeting, and see whether the content column changes your view.
Ask a colleague who was in the same meeting to list the content of what was said, without their impression, and compare it with yours.
Do the exercise for yourself after an interview or a pitch, and notice which column you were relying on to make your case.

drills.name: Name the Hidden Rules
steps: Choose a setting you know well: a client dinner, a team social, a formal event.
Write down ten unwritten rules a newcomer would need to know.
Mark which ones you learned without being told.
Share the list, privately and kindly, with someone new to that setting.
variations: Ask someone who is new to the setting which rules surprised them most, and add those to your list.
Turn your list into a short written guide for newcomers, and ask someone from a different background to check it for anything you missed.
Mark any rule on your list that exists mainly to show who belongs, and consider whether it is needed at all.

drills.name: Score the Content
steps: Before your next interview or assessment, write down what a strong answer to each question would contain.
During the conversation, note what was said, in the candidate's words.
Score against your list before forming an overall impression.
Compare your scores with your gut feeling, and note where they differ.
variations: Ask a second interviewer to score the same candidate independently, and compare your scores before discussing impressions.
Record the candidate's answer to one question word for word, and score it again a day later without your notes on manner.
Notice which candidates you warmed to during small talk, and check whether their scores matched your warmth.

drills.name: Accent Check
steps: Listen to a few voices you hear this week: colleagues, callers, people on television.
Notice any assumption you form about each speaker's intelligence or competence from their accent.
Ask what evidence you actually have for it.
Write one sentence about what you noticed.
variations: Listen to a radio interview with the presenter's introduction muted, and notice what you assume about the guest before you know who they are.
Notice which accents are used in advertisements for expensive products, and which for cheap ones.
Ask a colleague with a regional accent whether anyone has ever commented on it at work, and listen to the answer.

quiz.q: A manager says the candidate who leaned back, relaxed and unhurried, clearly has the most confidence and ability. What does this chapter suggest?
options: He is right, since relaxed ease in an interview reliably signals both competence and real confidence in the work
Relaxed disengagement is linked to class background, not ability, so it should not stand in for evidence
Leaning back always signals arrogance, so the candidate should be marked down for showing it
Interview posture is random and says nothing about anything, including where someone grew up
quiz.explain: Kraus and Keltner found that people from wealthier backgrounds showed more disengagement cues. Ease is a habit learned in a particular upbringing, not a measure of ability.

quiz.q: What did Kraus and Keltner find in their 2009 study of strangers getting acquainted?
options: Wealthier participants showed more disengagement, poorer participants more nods and laughs
Wealthier participants nodded and laughed more, while poorer participants doodled and fidgeted
There were no differences in behaviour between participants from different backgrounds
Observers could not estimate anyone's class from the clips, whatever cues were present
quiz.explain: Participants from wealthier backgrounds doodled, groomed and fiddled more, while those from poorer backgrounds nodded, laughed and looked at their partner more. Observers used these cues to estimate class better than chance.

quiz.q: What did Kraus and colleagues find in their 2019 study of speech and hiring?
options: Listeners needed several minutes of speech before they could judge anyone's class
Evaluators preferred working-class speakers, judging them more honest and hardworking
Class was judged from seven words, and higher-class speakers were offered more money
Word choice mattered far more than pronunciation in judging a speaker's class
quiz.explain: Listeners judged class from just seven words, mostly from pronunciation. Evaluators rated higher-class-sounding candidates as more competent and offered them higher salaries, without knowing their qualifications.

quiz.q: According to Rivera's study of elite firms, what did evaluators often mean by fit?
options: How well a candidate's qualifications matched the job description
How quickly a candidate could be trained to do the specific work required
How well a candidate would represent the firm's values to clients
Similarity to themselves, including shared leisure pursuits and style
quiz.explain: Fit often meant cultural similarity, including sports, travel and self-presentation, and it often outweighed concerns about productivity. Because those pursuits track wealth, fit tended to reproduce class.

quiz.q: At a client dinner, a new junior colleague uses his cutlery and napkin differently from everyone else. What fits this chapter best?
options: Say nothing at the table, and offer to explain the dinner codes privately if he wants
Correct him quietly at the table, so that the clients do not notice the mistake
Make a light joke about it, so that he knows nobody minds and can relax
Mention it to his manager afterwards, so that he can be given some training
quiz.explain: A different style is not an error, and public correction adds to the effort he is already making. Explaining unwritten rules privately, if he wants it, helps without humiliating.

quiz.q: You interviewed two candidates. One was polished and easy to talk to; the other was nervous, with a strong regional accent, but gave stronger answers. What fits this chapter best?
options: Hire the polished candidate, since clients will respond better to his manner
Score both against the criteria you set in advance, and decide on the answers
Hire the nervous candidate, since accents should always be favoured in hiring
Ask both back for a second, informal interview over lunch to see who fits in
quiz.explain: Structured scoring directs attention to what was said rather than how it sounded. An informal lunch would give class signals even more room to stand in for evidence.

quiz.q: What did the sociologist Norbert Elias trace about European rules of table manners?
options: That they were invented in the twentieth century by etiquette writers for the middle classes
That they spread from royal courts to the wealthy and then downward, marking who belonged
That they arose from medical advice about hygiene and had nothing to do with social status
That they were identical across Europe and have hardly changed since the Middle Ages
quiz.explain: Elias traced how rules about forks, napkins and not spitting spread from royal courts to the wealthy and then downward over centuries. Each new rule became a way of telling who belonged.

quiz.q: A consultant explains a man's test results to his daughter rather than to him, after hearing his strong regional accent. What fits this chapter best?
options: Carry on with the daughter, since she seems better placed to explain things to him later
Address the patient directly in plain language, and check his understanding in his own words
Speak to the patient more slowly and simply, since an accent suggests he will struggle
Give the patient written leaflets instead, since conversation is clearly difficult for him
quiz.explain: Listeners judge class from a few words and tend to rate higher-class speakers as more competent. An accent says nothing about a person's ability to understand, so speaking to him directly and checking his understanding is the fair reading.

quiz.q: Someone says that a candidate who nods and laughs a lot in a first meeting must be nervous and lacking in confidence. What does this chapter suggest?
options: That nodding and laughing are engagement cues that Kraus and Keltner linked with background, not confidence
That nodding and laughing are always signs of anxiety, whatever the person's background or upbringing
That candidates who nod and laugh are usually trying to manipulate the interviewer into liking them
That engagement cues mean nothing at all and should simply be ignored in every first meeting
quiz.explain: Kraus and Keltner found that people from poorer backgrounds tended to show more engagement cues, such as nodding and laughing. They reflect upbringing, not a lack of confidence or ability.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific moment when class shaped how you read someone, or how you were read: an interview, a dinner, a first day, a meeting with in-laws. Describe the signals involved: accent, manners, posture, clothing, the topics of conversation. What conclusion was drawn, and was it about upbringing or about ability? If you have moved between class worlds yourself, describe one code you had to learn, and one habit from your first world you have chosen to keep.
reflection.guidance: Class is rarely discussed openly, so it can take a moment to see it. Focus on specific behaviours rather than general impressions, and be honest about both directions: the times you were judged and the times you judged others. If nothing comes to mind, think about the last time someone's accent or table manners surprised you, and what you assumed about them in that first moment.

failureMode: The first failure is to read ease and polish as competence, when they mostly reflect upbringing. The second is to read eager attentiveness, nodding and laughing as nervousness or low status. The third is to judge people by accent, when class can be heard in seven words and costs candidates money. The fourth is to hire for fit, when fit often means similarity to yourself. The fifth is to correct someone's manners in front of others or treat a different style as an error. And the sixth, for those who have moved between worlds, is to treat the habits of your first world as faults to be erased rather than assets to keep.

moreCases.title: The patient the consultant talked past
moreCases.scene:
Terry, fifty-eight, worked for thirty years as a fitter at a car plant in the Midlands, and left school at sixteen. He has a strong local
  accent and a habit, when he is nervous, of nodding along and saying "Yeah, yeah" while people talk. He has been referred to a hospital consultant
  about a heart problem, and his daughter, Kerry, thirty, a pharmacist, comes with him.

  The consultant, Dr Hartley, is pleasant and efficient. Within a minute of the appointment starting, she has begun to address most of her
  explanation to Kerry. She explains the test results to her in medical terms, turns to Terry only to say, slowly and simply, "Your heart isn't
  pumping as well as it should," and then goes back to Kerry to discuss the options. When Terry asks a question about whether he can keep fishing, she
  answers it briefly, to him, and then asks Kerry whether her father understands the medication plan.

  Kerry is mortified. She says, "You'd better ask him. He's the one taking it." Dr Hartley apologises, a little flustered, and turns to Terry.

  On the drive home, Terry is quiet. Then he says that it happens all the time: in banks, at the council, at the garage when he takes the car in with
  Kerry. People hear him and decide he is thick.

He had also, Kerry knows, read every leaflet the GP gave him twice and written his questions on the back of an envelope, which is still in his coat pocket.

Dr Hartley had seen eleven patients that morning, and was running forty minutes late. Efficiency, under pressure, tends to follow the path of least resistance, and the path led to the person who sounded like her.

Terry had also, the week before, sat in the GP's waiting room rehearsing his questions under his breath, because he knew from experience that if he stumbled, people would stop listening to him.
moreCases.misread:
Dr Hartley read Terry's accent, his nodding and his "yeah, yeah" as signs that he would struggle to understand, and turned to the daughter whose speech sounded like hers. Terry read the consultant's turn away from him as being judged stupid, as he had been many times before.

Kerry, too, had been read: as the competent one, because her years of training had given her the consultant's vocabulary and something like the consultant's accent.

The consultant, asked later, said that she had been trying to be efficient, and had assumed the daughter would explain things better at home. She had not noticed that the assumption rested on a voice.

The receptionist at the clinic, who had greeted Terry warmly in a voice like his, had treated him exactly as he expected to be treated everywhere.
moreCases.betterRead:
Kraus and colleagues found that listeners could judge a speaker's class from seven words, mostly from pronunciation, and that people who sounded higher class were judged more competent. Kraus and Keltner found that people from poorer backgrounds tended to show more engagement cues, such as nodding, which observers read as a sign of class. Terry's nodding was attention, and his accent said nothing about his ability to understand his own heart. The better approach, which Dr Hartley adopted at his next appointment, was to address him directly, explain the results to him in plain language without talking down, ask what mattered most to him, and check his understanding by asking him to tell her the plan in his own words. Terry explained it perfectly. He also told her that he had been doing the fitting on heart-lung machines at the plant for ten years, and asked her an excellent question about the valve.

Kerry said afterwards that her father talked about the appointment for a week, and that being spoken to directly had mattered to him more than the diagnosis.

moreCases.title: The scholarship student at formal hall
moreCases.scene:
Shaun, eighteen, is the first person in his family to go to university, and he has won a place at an old college where students eat a formal
  dinner twice a week, in gowns, at long tables lit by candles. On his first night, he sits between two students who went to private schools. In
  front of him are three glasses, two knives, three forks, two spoons and a napkin folded into a shape he does not recognise. Everyone stands when a
  bell rings and someone says a grace in Latin.

  Shaun spends the whole meal watching. He waits for others to start before he eats, copies which fork they use, holds his glass the way they do and
  says very little, because he is afraid his accent and his small talk will give him away. When the student on his left asks where he went to school,
  he names his comprehensive and sees her pause for half a second before saying, "Oh, how nice."

  His tutor, Dr Okafor, sitting further down the table, notices that the new student seems stiff and unsmiling, and wonders whether he is unhappy or
  simply aloof. She makes a mental note that he might not be settling in.

  After dinner, Shaun goes back to his room and rings his mum, and tells her he is not sure he belongs there.

He had also, that afternoon, bought a new shirt for the dinner, the most expensive he had ever owned, and spent the meal worrying that he would spill something on it.

His mum tells him that she cleaned offices at a university like his for ten years, and that he has as much right to sit at that table as anyone who has ever sat there.

Earlier that day, at the freshers' fair, a society stall had asked him whether he had rowed at school. He had said no, and the student at the stall had turned to the next person in the queue.
moreCases.misread:
Dr Okafor read Shaun's stiffness and silence as unhappiness or aloofness. The student beside him read his school's name as a fact worth a pause. Shaun read the whole evening as a test he was failing, and his own careful watching as proof that he did not belong.

And Shaun read the pause as a verdict on him, when it may have been nothing more than a student who had never met anyone from a comprehensive before and did not know what to say.

The second-years at the end of the table, who had been through the same thing, read Shaun's stiffness accurately and said nothing, because nobody had said anything to them.

Shaun's mum, on the phone, read his worry as homesickness, until he told her about the cutlery and she laughed and said she would have had no idea either.
moreCases.betterRead:
Bourdieu's idea of habitus describes how manners learned in childhood feel natural to those who have them, and Elias traced how rules about cutlery and napkins became ways of telling who belonged. Shaun was not unhappy with the company; he was working hard to follow codes nobody had told him, and that effort showed as stiffness. The better response came from two directions. Dr Okafor, instead of noting him as a worry, invited him for a coffee, asked how he was finding it and told him plainly that she had been the first in her own family to go to university, and had spent her first formal dinner watching which fork to use. A second-year student from a similar background, whom she introduced him to, explained the rules before the next dinner, including the ones nobody tells you. At the third dinner, Shaun talked about football with a professor for twenty minutes.

Shaun later became the student who explained the rules to the new first-years, and added a few the college had never written down.

Dr Okafor also changed how the college briefed new students before their first formal dinner, so that nobody had to arrive guessing.

moreCases.title: The partner with no presence
moreCases.scene:
Sharon, forty-five, is a senior associate at an accountancy firm, and this is the third year she has been put forward for partnership. She grew
  up on a council estate in Leeds, went to the local comprehensive and trained through an apprenticeship rather than a degree. Her clients love her,
  and her figures are the best in her department. Each year, the partnership committee has turned her down with the same feedback: she needs to work on
  her presence.

  Nobody has told her what presence means. When she asks, she is told that partners need to be comfortable in any room, that clients need to see a
  certain polish, and that she might like to come to the annual golf day, which she has never been invited to before. She notices that the two men
  promoted last year both play golf, both went to the same university as the senior partner, and both, as far as she can see, have smaller client
  books than hers.

  She goes to the golf day. She cannot play, spends the afternoon in the clubhouse and feels, by the end of it, more out of place than ever.

  A new partner on the committee, Rohan, who joined from another firm, reads her file and asks the committee, at the next meeting, what exactly her
  presence is lacking.

She has also noticed that the partners talk about clients differently from the way she does: in terms of relationships and lunches, where she talks about problems and fees. She has wondered whether that is what they mean.

She has also, over the years, been mistaken twice at client events for a member of the catering staff, and once asked to fetch more coffee.

At the golf day, she noticed that the senior partner spent most of the afternoon with the two men promoted the year before, and that the conversations on the course seemed to be about clients as well as golf.
moreCases.misread:
The committee read Sharon's directness, her regional accent and her absence from the golf course as a lack of presence and polish. They read the ease of the candidates who shared their background as readiness for partnership.

She also read the feedback, for three years, as being about her, and worked hard on her manner, when the problem was in the criteria the committee was using.

The two men who were promoted had read their own ease at the golf day as merit, and would have been surprised to hear it called a head start.

Rohan, coming from outside, could see the pattern that the committee could not, because he did not share the background that made the pattern feel natural.
moreCases.betterRead:
Rivera found that evaluators at elite firms placed great weight on fit, which often meant similarity in leisure pursuits and style, and that those markers were closely tied to wealth and upbringing. "Presence" can work in the same way: a word that sounds like a skill and turns out, when examined, to mean manner. Sharon's clients and figures were the evidence that mattered, and the feedback asked her to acquire a background rather than a capability. Rohan's better approach was to ask for specifics, as this book recommends with any vague judgment. Nobody on the committee could name a client who had found Sharon lacking. The committee agreed to assess partnership candidates against written criteria, with evidence, and to stop using "presence" unless it could be described in behaviour. Sharon was made partner that spring. She has not been to the golf day since.

She also asked the committee to publish the criteria to all associates, so that the next candidate would not have to guess.

Rohan also asked that every partnership feedback letter include at least one specific example, which ended the use of "presence" almost overnight.

moreCases.title: The finance director who flattened his voice
moreCases.scene:
Stephen, fifty, grew up on an estate in Sunderland, the son of a shipyard welder. He won a place at university, trained as an accountant and is
  now finance director of a large retailer in London. Somewhere in his twenties he flattened his accent. He did it deliberately, after a manager told
  him, kindly, that he would go further if he sounded "less regional". He also learned to wine and dine, to play the small-talk game and to dress the
  part.

  It worked. But Stephen has never felt entirely at ease at work. He watches himself in every meeting. He is careful, polished and a little distant,
  and colleagues describe him as impressive but hard to know. He has noticed that the only times he is truly relaxed at work are on site visits to the
  warehouses, talking to the drivers and pickers, when his old voice comes back without his permission.

  At home in Sunderland for his father's seventieth birthday, his cousins tease him about having "gone posh". His father, who is proud of him, says
  nothing, but Stephen notices that he talks to him slightly more carefully than he talks to anyone else in the room.

  On the train back, Stephen realises that he has become a man who is slightly foreign in both places, and that he is tired.

He has also noticed, recently, that he flinches slightly when he hears his own voice in recordings of meetings, because it sounds like someone he has made up.

He has also noticed that he never mentions his background at work, and that colleagues who know him well assume he grew up somewhere much like them.

He has also noticed that, when he goes back to the estate, he still knows exactly how to stand at the bar and how to take a joke, and that those skills, which nobody at work values, have never left him.
moreCases.misread:
Stephen's colleagues read his careful polish as reserve, and his family read his flattened voice as distance. Stephen had read his first world's habits, his accent, his directness, his warmth, as faults to be corrected, and had corrected them so well that he no longer felt at home anywhere.

His cousins' teasing read his success as a betrayal, and his father's carefulness read it as a distance to be respected. Neither was what Stephen wanted.

The manager who gave him the advice twenty years earlier had read his accent as a barrier, and had been partly right about the room and wrong about the man.

Stephen's team, for their part, read his careful distance as seniority, and kept their own distance in return.
moreCases.betterRead:
Kraus and colleagues found that higher-class-sounding candidates were offered higher salaries, so the manager's advice to Stephen was not wrong about the cost. But this chapter suggests that the habits of a first world are not errors, and that it is worth deciding consciously which codes to adopt and which to keep. Stephen's better path, which he took slowly, was not to throw away what he had learned but to stop hiding where he came from. He let his accent come back a little in meetings and found that nobody objected. He brought the directness and warmth he had grown up with into his team, and they responded to it. He talked to his father about the welding, at length. And he started a mentoring scheme for apprentices from the warehouses, explaining the unwritten rules of head office plainly, as nobody had explained them to him.

At his father's next birthday, his cousins said he sounded more like himself, and his father talked to him about the shipyard for most of the evening.

workedReading.title: Hosting a client dinner with a new trainee
workedReading.scene:
Victoria, forty-eight, is a partner at a law firm, and next Thursday she is taking a client, the general counsel of a manufacturing company, to dinner, along with a trainee, Kyle, twenty-four. Kyle is one of the best trainees the firm has had in years. He grew up in a small town in Essex, went to the local sixth form and studied law at a university that is not one of the usual ones for the firm. He has never been to a client dinner, and Victoria noticed that he went pale when she mentioned it. She remembers her own first client dinner, as the daughter of a teacher and a bus driver, and the moment she drank from the wrong glass. She wants Kyle to spend the evening thinking about the client, not about the cutlery.

She has also noticed that Kyle laughs very easily and nods a great deal when she talks to him, which she now reads, after this chapter, as attention rather than nerves.

She also knows that the client is a man who values plain speaking, and that Kyle's directness, which some partners find raw, may be exactly what he likes.

She also knows that Kyle has been turning down after-work drinks, and suspects that cost is part of the reason. She makes sure the firm's policy on paying for client entertainment is clear to him.

steps.label: Explain the evening beforehand
steps.text:
On Monday, she takes Kyle for a coffee and tells him exactly how the evening will go: where they will meet, what to wear, who will be there, roughly what they will talk about, how long it will take and that the firm pays. She mentions, lightly, the things nobody ever explains: start with the outside cutlery, the bread plate is on the left, it is fine to say no to wine, and she will order first. He writes it all down. She tells him that she learned all of it by getting it wrong.

She also tells him that it is fine to ask her quietly during the evening if he is unsure about anything, and agrees a small signal he can use.

She also tells him that the client is far more interested in the planning issue than in anyone's table manners, which turns out to be true.

steps.label: Choose a gentler venue
steps.text:
She chooses a good restaurant that is relaxed rather than formal, with a set menu and no wine ritual, where the codes are lighter for everyone. She knows that the client, who grew up on a farm, will probably prefer it too. Manners work as a gate, this chapter says; she can choose where to hold the meeting so that the gate is lower.

She also books a table in a quieter corner, so that the conversation can be heard without anyone raising their voice.

She also checks the menu online in advance and sends it to Kyle, so that he can choose before he arrives rather than reading an unfamiliar menu under pressure.

steps.label: Set the pace at the table
steps.text:
At the table, she sits so that Kyle can see what she does without having to watch for it. She picks up her napkin first, orders first and starts eating first, so that he has a model without having to ask. When the client orders a beer rather than wine, Victoria orders one too, and Kyle, visibly relieved, does the same.

She also avoids the elaborate tasting menu and asks for the ordinary one, which removes several decisions from the evening.

She also leaves her phone in her bag, which tells Kyle that he can leave his there too, without having to wonder.

She also notices that she has slowed her own pace at the table, which seems to slow everyone, and gives Kyle time to follow.

steps.label: Model rather than correct
steps.text:
At one point Kyle uses his knife to push food onto his fork, which is not quite how the client does it. Victoria does nothing, says nothing and does not look. Correcting someone's manners in front of others, as this chapter warns, turns a small difference into a public lesson. If anything needed saying, she would say it privately, kindly and later. Nothing does.

She knows that the client almost certainly did not notice, and that if he did, he did not care. People notice manners far less than the person worrying about them believes.

She also notices that she herself still holds her glass by the bowl rather than the stem, and that nobody in thirty years has ever mentioned it.

steps.label: Bring him into the conversation
steps.text:
She makes sure Kyle has something to contribute. When the conversation turns to the client's new factory, she says, "Kyle did the research on the planning issue, he knows more about it than I do," and turns towards him. He talks for five minutes, clearly and precisely, and the client asks him two follow-up questions. Victoria notices that his accent becomes stronger when he relaxes, and that the client, who has a strong Yorkshire accent of his own, seems to like him more for it.

She also asks Kyle afterwards what he enjoyed most about the evening, and he says the planning question. She makes a note to give him more of that work.

She also asks the client a question about his own career, which leads him to mention that he left school at sixteen. Kyle visibly relaxes.

steps.label: Handle the bill quietly
steps.text:
She has arranged in advance for the bill to be settled at the bar, so that there is no awkward moment at the table. When the client offers to contribute, she thanks him and says it is the firm's pleasure. She tells Kyle in the taxi that this is how she always does it, so that he will know next time.

She also explains, in the taxi, how the firm's entertainment budget works, so that he will not be anxious about money if he ever hosts a dinner himself.

She also thanks the client for his time in a way that Kyle can hear and copy, which is the last of the unwritten rules of the evening.

In the taxi, Kyle asks her what she got wrong at her first dinner, and she tells him about the glass. They both laugh.

steps.label: What happened
steps.text:
The client emails the next day to thank Victoria for a very pleasant evening, and asks whether Kyle could work on the next phase of the planning matter. Kyle tells Victoria that he had expected to spend the dinner terrified, and instead spent it talking about the work. She writes down the list she gave him over coffee, tidies it and sends it to the head of trainees, suggesting that every new trainee should get it.

She also remembers, writing the list, how much she would have given for one at twenty-four.

The head of trainees adds the list to the induction pack, and two other partners start using it for their own trainees.

moreFailures.title: Mistaking directness for rudeness
moreFailures.body:
Many people from working-class backgrounds grow up with a direct style of speaking: saying what they think, plainly, without the cushioning phrases that are common in middle-class professional settings. "That won't work" rather than "I wonder whether we might consider an alternative". In rooms where cushioning is the norm, directness can be read as rude, aggressive or unsophisticated, and the person who uses it can be marked down for tone rather than content. But directness is a style, not a flaw, and in many situations it is more useful than the alternative, because everyone knows where they stand. Before reacting to how something was said, ask whether it was true and useful. If you need a different register in a particular setting, such as with a client, say so plainly, as you would want to be told. And notice which styles in your workplace are treated as the default and which as a deviation.

It also helps to notice whose directness is called "refreshing" and whose is called "abrasive" in your workplace.

Many teams find, once they stop marking it down, that directness saves them time and confusion.

moreFailures.title: Reading polish as arrogance
moreFailures.body:
Class readings can cut the other way too. Some people, especially those who have felt looked down on, read ease, polish or an upper-class accent as arrogance, insincerity or entitlement, and treat people who have them with suspicion. It is an understandable reaction, but it is the same mistake in reverse: judging someone's character from the habits of their upbringing rather than from what they do. A man who leans back relaxed in a meeting may be arrogant, or may simply have been raised in rooms like this one. A public-school accent tells you where someone went to school, not whether they are kind, honest or good at their job. The principle of this chapter applies in every direction: notice class signals, and keep them separate from your judgment of the person, which should rest on evidence.

If you notice yourself bristling at someone's accent or manner, run the same check you would run in the other direction.

A good test is to ask whether you would describe the same behaviour in the same way if the accent were different.

moreFailures.title: Asking where people went to school
moreFailures.body:
"Where did you go to school?" and "What does your father do?" can be innocent questions. In some settings they work as sorting devices, placing a person in a class hierarchy within seconds and setting the tone of everything that follows, as the student beside Shaun showed with her half-second pause. For someone from a less privileged background, the question can feel like a test they are about to fail, and many learn to dread it. If you are curious about someone, ask about things that do not rank them: what they are working on, what they enjoy, where they live now, what brought them here. If they want to tell you about their school or their family, they will. And if you hear the question being used as a sorting device, change the subject.

If someone asks you the question and you would rather not answer, it is fine to say where you live now, and move on.

In a hiring process, these questions have no place at all.

moreFailures.title: Teaching the codes as if they were virtues
moreFailures.body:
Mentors and managers who want to help people from less privileged backgrounds often explain the unwritten rules, which is valuable, as Victoria did. The trap is to present them as right rather than as conventions: to suggest that a regional accent needs fixing, that directness is unprofessional, or that the way the senior partners eat, dress or talk is simply the correct way. That tells the person that where they come from is a problem to be solved. A better framing explains the rules as the local customs of a particular setting, worth knowing in the way it is worth knowing the customs of a country you are visiting, and leaves the person free to decide which to adopt. It also helps to say, as Victoria did, that you had to learn them too, if you did, and to question the rules that exist mainly to keep people out.

A good test is whether you would be comfortable explaining the rule to someone from another country as a local custom.

And if a rule has no purpose other than marking who belongs, consider whether your organisation still needs it.

questions.q: Is it wrong to notice someone's class?
questions.a:
No, and it would be almost impossible not to. Kraus and Keltner found that observers could estimate social class from sixty seconds of silent behaviour, and Kraus and colleagues found that seven words were enough from speech. Noticing happens in seconds and mostly without intention. The problem this chapter describes is not noticing but ranking: letting accent, polish, ease or manners stand in for judgments of intelligence, skill, honesty or effort. The practical habit is to separate the two, as the Ease Versus Evidence drill suggests. Notice the signal, name it to yourself as information about upbringing, and then make your judgment of the person on what they have actually said and done, preferably against criteria set in advance.

It also helps to notice your own reactions to your own accent and manners, which can be harsher than anyone else's.

And notice when the signal flatters you as well as when it disadvantages others. Both are worth checking.

And if you notice someone else ranking, a simple question about the evidence often changes the conversation.

questions.q: Should I change my accent for work?
questions.a:
That is your choice, and there is no single right answer. Kraus and colleagues found that candidates who sounded higher class were offered higher salaries by evaluators who knew nothing about their qualifications, so the cost of an accent can be real. But that cost reflects the bias of listeners, not a flaw in the speaker, and many people keep their accents and do very well. Stephen flattened his and found, years later, that it had cost him something too. Speaking clearly, at a pace others can follow, helps in any accent. Beyond that, decide consciously what you want to keep and what you want to adapt, rather than letting discomfort decide. If you are a manager, the more useful question is whether your organisation is rewarding accents rather than ability.

If you do adapt, it can help to keep your first voice somewhere: with family, with old friends, in the places where it belongs.

It also helps to remember that people with strong regional accents are often better understood than they fear.

questions.q: How can I help a new colleague who does not know the unwritten rules?
questions.a:
Tell them, privately, kindly and in advance, as Victoria and Charles did. Explain how a client dinner works, what the dress code really means, how meetings tend to run, who to copy into what, how the bill is handled and any other customs that newcomers would otherwise learn by getting them wrong in public. Frame the rules as local customs rather than as the right way to behave. Mention that you had to learn them too, if you did. Then, in the setting itself, model rather than correct: do things first, so that they can follow without watching anxiously, and never correct their manners in front of others. Finally, bring them into the conversation by giving them something to contribute, which turns attention from their manners to their mind.

And once they know the rules, let them decide which ones to follow. Knowledge of a custom is not an obligation to adopt it.

It also helps to tell them which rules are flexible and which really matter, so that they can spend their attention wisely.

questions.q: Why do people from wealthier backgrounds sometimes seem less attentive?
questions.a:
Kraus and Keltner found that, in conversations between strangers, participants from wealthier, more educated backgrounds showed more signs of disengagement, such as doodling, grooming and fiddling with objects, while participants from poorer backgrounds showed more engagement, such as nodding and laughing. The researchers suggested that people with more resources depend less on others and can afford to attend less closely, while people with fewer resources have more reason to stay attuned. This is a pattern across groups, not a description of any individual, and it is not a judgment of character. But it is worth knowing in two directions: a candidate's eager nodding is not nervousness or low status, and a senior colleague's apparent inattention may be habit rather than contempt.

It can also help, if you are from a wealthier background, to notice your own habits of attention and make a point of showing interest.

It is also worth remembering that a pattern across groups says nothing certain about the person in front of you.

And if a senior colleague seems inattentive to you, ask a direct question. You may find that he was listening all along.

questions.q: How can I avoid hiring for fit?
questions.a:
Decide in advance what the job requires, and judge candidates against that rather than against your sense of whether they would be good company. Use structured interviews, with set questions and scored answers, as Part IV described. Write down what a strong answer would contain before you hear any. Notice the moment of recognition, the feeling that a candidate is someone like you, and treat it as a reason to check your scores, as Charles learned to. Be wary of conversations about shared hobbies, schools or holidays, which Rivera found often tipped decisions at elite firms. If your organisation values culture, define what that means in behaviour, such as how people treat colleagues or handle mistakes, rather than in style. And look at who you have hired over the past few years, and ask how many of them resemble you.

It also helps to involve people from different backgrounds in setting the criteria, so that the definition of good is not set by one group.

It is also worth asking new hires, after a few months, what nearly put them off applying, and acting on what they say.

questions.q: What can I do if I feel out of place in formal or upper-class settings?
questions.a:
First, know that the feeling is common and has a cause. The codes of these settings are learned, not innate, and people who grew up with them follow them without effort, which makes them invisible. Your effort shows only because you are doing work that others are not. Second, prepare: ask someone you trust to explain how the evening or the meeting will run, as Shaun's second-year friend did. Third, remember that the habits you bring, such as attentiveness, warmth and directness, are assets in most rooms, and that most people are far more interested in what you say than in which fork you use. And finally, look for allies, others who have made the same move, who can share what they learned and remind you that you belong.

It can also help to remember that many people in those rooms feel out of place too, and are simply better at hiding it.

If a setting continues to feel unwelcoming after you have learned its codes, that may say more about the setting than about you.

watch.title: Titanic: First Class Dinner
watch.notice: A steerage passenger at a first-class dinner. Notice how he watches the others for the codes, how the diners read his manners, and how much of the scene is about cutlery, posture and timing rather than words.

watch.title: Parasite: Official Trailer
watch.notice: A poor family infiltrates a wealthy household. Notice the small physical giveaways of class the film turns on: posture, manners and, famously, smell, and how carefully the family performs the codes of the house.

reviewPrompt: This week, separate one person's manner from their substance, and explain one unwritten rule to someone new.
